opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Malik, thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, and we don't work for any company, union or party. Nothing you tell me will be linked to your name, so feel free to tell me what you'd say out loud and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, let's go. I've got a client at six, so we're good till then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI's cool for making meal plans, but it can't spot your squat or yell at you on the last rep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes. Apps have been around forever. People still pay me because they need someone to show up for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep building my client list, use an AI app for programmes and captions, and post more on Instagram to get new people in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Chill. All good.

S0.say: AI's cool for meal plans, but it can't spot your squat or push you on the last rep.
S0.think: Nothing changes; people still pay for someone to show up for.
S0.do: Builds his client list, uses AI for programmes and captions, and posts more to attract clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say same thing. The fitness apps get smarter, but people don't stick with apps. They stick with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd use the smarter tools to run more clients at once. Online coaching with check-ins, that kind of thing. More money for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start an online coaching side thing, like twenty clients paying monthly. Use AI to write the plans and I do the video check-ins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Kind of hyped.

S1.say: The apps get smarter, but people stick with people, not apps.
S1.think: Smarter tools would let him coach more clients at once and earn more.
S1.do: Starts an online coaching side business with AI-written plans and video check-ins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if you lost your desk job, come to the gym. Get strong, clear your head. I'd probably run a deal for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Office people are a lot of my clients. Some would cancel because money's tight. But some would have more time to train. Could be a wash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do a discounted package for people between jobs, so I keep them. Push the online side harder. Maybe pick up a group class or two for steady money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Little bit of watching the bookings.

S2.say: Lost your desk job? Come to the gym, get strong and clear your head.
S2.think: Office clients might cancel to save money, but some would have more time to train.
S2.do: Offers a discount package for people between jobs, pushes online coaching, and adds group classes for steady pay.
S2.feel: Fine, keeping an eye on bookings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say physical stuff is the future. Your body is the one thing AI can't do for you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lots of my clients would lose their jobs and cut me first. I'm a luxury. But the people getting rich from shares would want a trainer more than ever. I'd have to chase them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go after higher-end clients, maybe get into a fancy gym downtown. Get a nutrition certificate so I can charge more. Cut back on going out, since I've got no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've got no savings. How long could you go if bookings dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a month, maybe two. That's why I'd move fast. I'm not gonna sit and wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit stressed. But I'm young, I'll figure it out.

S3.say: Physical stuff is the future. Your body is the one thing AI can't do for you.
S3.think: Many clients would cut him as a luxury, but people getting rich from shares would want trainers more.
S3.do: Chases wealthier clients at a high-end gym, gets a nutrition certificate, and cuts back on going out.
S3.feel: A bit stressed, but confident he'll figure it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a robot can carry boxes, sure, but nobody wants a robot telling them to do one more set. People train with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots don't really hit my job. But everybody being out of work hits my clients. Then again, people with no job and nothing to do might want the gym more. I'd bet on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the last one. And I'd try pitching cheap group sessions to the city or community centres, for people who lost work. Keep the online side going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Little uneasy. Still feel like I'm on the right side of it.

S4.say: A robot can carry boxes, but nobody wants a robot telling them to do one more set.
S4.think: Robots don't touch his job, and people with no work might want the gym more, though his clients' money would suffer.
S4.do: Sticks with the same plan and pitches cheap group sessions to community centres for people out of work.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, still feels on the right side of it.
